name: Restylane Vital / Skinboosters

card.summary: Galderma's small-dose hyaluronic acid injections placed in the skin to improve elasticity and texture; the longest-studied skin booster, mostly in small clinical studies.
card.aka: Restylane Skinboosters Vital, Vital Light, NASHA, hydrofilling
card.note: Most studies are small and several are single-arm; effects are described as temporary.

quick.overview:
Restylane Vital is a stabilised hyaluronic acid gel (NASHA) made by Q-Med/Galderma that is injected as many tiny deposits in the skin to improve its quality, such as elasticity and hydration, rather than to add volume. It sits at the centre of the 'skin booster' category.

Studies since 2008 have measured changes in elasticity and appearance on the face, neck, hands and elsewhere, generally in small groups. In Korea the technique is also called hydrofilling.
quick.mechanism: Clinicians place small amounts of gel in the mid-dermis with a needle, a cannula or a specialised injector. The hyaluronic acid binds water and is described as improving hydration and elasticity.
quick.risks: Reported effects are usually temporary swelling, redness, bruising and small lumps. A case report describes persistent nodules on the neck after HA filler. Hyaluronic acid fillers carry rarer risks such as granulomas and vascular complications, and the procedure is performed by clinicians.

lead: Restylane Vital, part of the Restylane Skinboosters line, is a stabilised hyaluronic acid-based gel of non-animal origin (NASHA) injected into the dermis in small amounts to improve skin quality such as elasticity and smoothness.[1][2] Restylane is made by Galderma and was the first hyaluronic acid filler approved by the US FDA for cosmetic injection into facial tissue.[3]

The 'skin booster' concept developed as hyaluronic acid products were repurposed from volume filling to dermal conditioning.[2] A 2008 study reported rejuvenating effects on facial skin,[1] and a 2010 pilot measured skin elasticity after three sessions in 19 patients.[4] Later work covers the nasojugal groove, neck, hands and acne scars.[5][6][7][8]
The technique has been described by Wikipedia as having been popularised by a 2007 'fern pattern' approach from Dutch doctor Tom van Eijk to restore dermal elasticity.[3]

paras: Skin boosters are defined in a 2024 review as hyaluronic acid products used to improve dermal condition, with Restylane Vital cited as a repurposed example.[2] Delivery options in studies include a specialised injector and micropuncture technique.[4][5][9]
Studies have applied Vital to the face, neck, dorsal hands and décolletage, and trials include acne scars and post-menopausal skin.[1][7][8][10][11][12][13]

A 2008 clinical and biophysical study of mid-dermal NASHA reported effects on appearance and elasticity of facial skin.[1] A 2010 pilot of three sessions spaced four weeks apart in the lower cheeks measured viscoelastic skin parameters in 19 patients.[4] A randomised split-face study in ten Korean women compared treatment of the nasojugal groove using Restylane Vital with a specialised injector.[5] Further studies examined facial hydrofilling,[6] neck rejuvenation combined with a non-ablative laser,[7] and hand augmentation.[8]

Registered trials include dorsal-hand studies,[10][11] acne scars,[13] facial studies,[14][15][16] a post-menopausal skin study[17] and a décolletage study.[12] A review of small-particle hyaluronic acid in plastic surgery also exists.[9]

Wikipedia lists temporary bruising, swelling and numbness, and rarely lumps or granulomas, which hyaluronidase can reverse, for Restylane products.[3] A 2025 case report described persistent nodules on the neck following hyaluronic acid filler.[18]

timeline.event: Dutch doctor Tom van Eijk's 'fern pattern' technique described for restoring dermal elasticity.[3]
Study of stabilised HA gel on facial skin aging published.[1]
Pilot study of three-session elasticity treatment published.[4]
